turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Contemptuously, you say? And I suppose you believe your disdain lends your pronouncements some sort of authority? Pray, enlighten me, Mr. Darcy; what *exactly* were Wickham's 'great misfortunes,' and why are you so eager to dismiss them?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Need I elaborate further, Miss Bennet? Mr. Wickham’s misfortunes, as you term them, are largely the consequence of his own dissolute and deceitful nature, a truth I shall demonstrate with documented evidence if you insist on perpetuating this… fanciful narrative.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Documented evidence, Mr. Darcy? How very… novel. I confess, I had assumed you would rely on the usual methods of character assassination, rather than resorting to the tedious formality of proof. Do you believe a pile of papers will somehow erase the charm and apparent sincerity that has, however misguidedly, captivated others?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your levity, Miss Bennet, is quite misplaced. It is not my intention to assassinate character, but to defend truth and propriety, qualities which, I observe, appear to be in short supply within your circle. I am weary of these frivolous debates and, frankly, compelled to address the matter which truly occupies my thoughts.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Propriety? From *you*, Mr. Darcy? It is rather amusing to hear you lecture on propriety, considering your own… interventions in the lives of others. I daresay a little less lecturing and a little more self-reflection might serve you better.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your barbs, while undoubtedly spirited, reveal a profound misunderstanding of my actions and motivations. I assure you, any 'interventions' were undertaken with the utmost consideration for what I believed to be the moral good, however imperfectly executed. And now, I must speak plainly, despite the provocation: I love you, Miss Bennet.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Love? Mr. Darcy, you jest, I presume. Such a declaration from a gentleman who has so consistently displayed a disdain for my family and, indeed, for anyone he deems beneath his notice… it requires a certain… audacity, wouldn’t you agree?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Audacity, Miss Bennet? Perhaps. But I am not given to jesting, particularly regarding matters of the heart. My feelings are not a performance for your amusement, but a sincere, albeit inconvenient, truth that I can no longer suppress.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Love, Mr. Darcy? You mistake my amusement for acceptance, I assure you. I find it difficult to credit such a sentiment from a man who considers my family so utterly beneath him, and whose actions have consistently demonstrated a profound lack of respect for anyone of… less consequence.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your continued insistence on dwelling upon past grievances is, I confess, disheartening. While I acknowledge that my actions have, at times, been misconstrued, to attribute them solely to disdain or disrespect is a gross oversimplification, and a deliberate misrepresentation of my intentions. Must you persist in this… adversarial posture, or might you grant me the courtesy of a more reasoned consideration?

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: A reasoned consideration, you say? From me, Mr. Darcy? After you’ve systematically dismantled my sister’s happiness and presumed to dictate the lives of everyone within a ten-mile radius? I daresay, sir, you’ve asked rather a great deal.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your accusations are… wounding. I will not deny that I have acted with a degree of… firmness, particularly when the well-being of those I care for is at stake. However, to characterize my actions as systematic dismantling and dictation is a distortion born of prejudice, and I find it profoundly unfair.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Prejudice, Mr. Darcy? I believe the prejudice lies squarely with you, judging individuals based on their connections and fortune rather than their character. Pray tell, what 'well-being' were you so desperately protecting that required you to interfere in my sister's affections and insult the sensibilities of my entire family?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your accusations are, as I have stated, deeply unfair. My concern for Miss King stemmed from a sincere belief that her prospects would be diminished by a union with a gentleman of considerably fewer resources and social standing – a consideration, I assure you, motivated by genuine solicitude, not by a desire to dictate.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Solicitude? You cloak your arrogance in the guise of concern, Mr. Darcy! To presume to know what is best for another, particularly a young woman of spirit, is an insult in itself – and one that reveals far more about your own elevated opinion of yourself than it does about Miss King’s supposed lack of prospects.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I perceive your continued inclination towards misrepresentation. While I concede that my actions may appear overbearing, I assure you they are rooted in a profound sense of duty and a desire to prevent demonstrable harm, not in mere arrogance as you so readily assert. I find myself compelled, however, to address the matter which truly occupies my thoughts - a matter that transcends these petty grievances.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Duty, Mr. Darcy? Is that what you call meddling in the lives of others? I daresay you mistake your own pride for a sense of obligation, and your interference for benevolence – a common failing amongst those of your station.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your persistent misinterpretations are becoming… vexing. While I am prepared to defend my actions, I find myself increasingly driven to express a truth that has long lain suppressed, a truth which, I fear, you are presently determined to misunderstand.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: A truth, Mr. Darcy? Pray, do enlighten me. I find myself increasingly curious to see what fresh justification for your intrusions you will attempt to conjure, though I confess my expectations are not high.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I will not indulge further in this cyclical exchange of accusations. I am speaking of my regard for you – a regard which has, despite your evident reluctance to acknowledge it, grown into a profound and undeniable affection. I am, in short, Miss Bennet, deeply and irrevocably in love with you.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: She answered him with cold civility.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His sense of her inferiority, of its being a degradation, of the family obstacles which judgment had always opposed to inclination, were dwelt on with a warmth which seemed due to the consequence he was wounding, but was very unlikely to recommend his suit.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: He concluded with representing to her the strength of that attachment which in spite of all his endeavours he had found impossible to conquer; and with expressing his hope that it would now be rewarded by her acceptance of his hand.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His misfortunes! repeated Darcy, contemptuously--yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
